subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on networks, protocols and packet switching, then mark my answer against the CCEA spec.
promptWeak: Explain LANs, WANs, protocols and packet switching for GCSE CCEA Computer Science simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What does LAN stand for?
questions.explain: LAN stands for Local Area Network, which covers a small geographical area such as one building or site.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of a WAN?
options: Two laptops sharing files by Bluetooth
The internet connecting sites across countries
questions.explain: A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a large geographical area across towns or countries; the internet is the largest example.

questions.q: Who typically owns and controls the infrastructure of a LAN?
questions.explain: A LAN's cabling and hardware are usually owned and managed by the single organisation that operates it, unlike a WAN which often uses third-party lines.

questions.q: In a star topology, how are the devices connected?
options: Every device connects directly to every other device
Each device connects to a central switch or hub
questions.explain: In a star topology every device has its own connection to a central node (switch/hub), so a single cable fault affects only one device.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of a star topology over a bus topology?
options: A single cable fault does not bring down the whole network
questions.explain: In a star, each device has its own link to the central switch, so one broken cable only disconnects that device rather than the whole network.

questions.q: Which is generally an advantage of a wired connection over a wireless one?
options: Faster and more reliable, more secure connection
questions.explain: Wired (e.g. Ethernet/fibre) connections are typically faster, more reliable and harder to intercept than wireless, though less convenient for mobility.

questions.q: Which technology provides short-range wireless connection between nearby devices?
questions.explain: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology used to connect nearby devices such as headphones or a phone to a speaker.

questions.q: What is the main job of a network switch?
options: To provide electrical power to devices
To store all files on the network
To forward data only to the device it is addressed to
To convert analogue signals to sound
questions.explain: A switch reads the destination MAC address and forwards each frame only to the intended device, reducing unnecessary traffic.

questions.q: What is the main role of a router?
options: To connect different networks together and direct data between them
To split one cable into many sockets
questions.explain: A router connects separate networks (such as a home LAN and the internet) and routes data packets between them using IP addresses.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a MAC address?
options: A unique physical address built into a device's network hardware
A temporary address given by the router
questions.explain: A MAC address is a unique hardware (physical) address assigned to a network interface by the manufacturer; it does not normally change.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid IPv4 address?
questions.explain: An IPv4 address is four numbers 0-255 separated by dots. 192.168.0.15 is valid; 300 and 256 are out of range, and the last is a MAC-style value.

questions.q: How does an IP address differ from a MAC address?
options: An IP address can change depending on the network; a MAC address is fixed to the hardware
A MAC address changes each time; an IP address never does
They are exactly the same thing
questions.explain: An IP address is assigned by the network and can change, whereas a MAC address is a fixed physical identifier burned into the device's hardware.

questions.q: What is a network protocol?
options: A set of rules that governs how data is transmitted
questions.explain: A protocol is an agreed set of rules that controls how devices communicate and transmit data across a network.

questions.q: Which protocol is used to transfer web pages between a web server and a browser?
questions.explain: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is used to request and transfer web pages; HTTPS adds encryption for security.

questions.q: In packet switching, how is a large message sent across a network?
options: Only over a single fixed cable
Split into small packets sent separately and reassembled at the destination
questions.explain: Packet switching breaks data into small packets that travel independently (possibly by different routes) and are reassembled in the correct order at the destination.

questions.q: Why is packet switching a robust way to send data?
options: If one route is busy or fails, packets can take alternative routes
It only works on one computer
questions.explain: Because packets are routed independently, they can be sent around congested or failed links, making the network more reliable.

questions.q: What does a DNS (Domain Name System) server do?
options: Translates a domain name into an IP address
questions.explain: DNS translates human-readable domain names (like example.com) into the numerical IP address needed to locate the server.

questions.q: What is 'phishing'?
options: Tricking users into revealing personal data via fake emails or websites
questions.explain: Phishing uses fake but convincing emails or websites to trick people into giving away passwords, card numbers or other personal data.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of malware?
options: A virus that copies itself and damages files
questions.explain: Malware is malicious software; a virus that replicates and damages or corrupts files is a classic example.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of encryption when sending data over a network?
options: To back up the data automatically
To scramble data so it is unreadable if intercepted
questions.explain: Encryption scrambles data using a key so that anyone who intercepts it cannot understand it without the correct decryption key.
